source.title: Arithmetic with Language Models: from Memorization to Computation

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains small language models on binary addition and multiplication and explicitly reports that no grokking was observed: training and validation accuracy remain close. This challenges the delayed-generalization pattern in V1 in the tested setup.
record.gate_note: The study also reports random-output controls, accuracy under alternative validation-region splits, representation correlations, amnesic probing, and architecture ablations. The random-output control is not an algorithmic task; the region-split results report final generalization rather than the delayed-accuracy pattern; the interpretability and ablation results do not test the listed versions. These are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: Small transformers trained from scratch on binary addition and multiplication. The paper reports training and validation accuracy curves and states that no grokking was observed. This bears on V1 in a new algorithmic setting. It is a side observation at a high training fraction (75%), not a targeted test of V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that small LMs learn binary addition and multiplication and generalize to unseen operands without memorization. They hold that the models act as Encoding-Regression-Decoding machines, regressing in value space. The 'no grokking' statement is a one-line side remark in Section 4.1, not a main conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses fixed-length, little-endian binary addition and multiplication, trained on a random 3/4 split, rather than the modular-arithmetic grokking setup. It trains a 701K-parameter encoder-decoder Transformer and a 298K-parameter nanoGPT model.
record.method_sensitivity: The validation-set construction changes final generalization: the value-space region split lowers final accuracy relative to the random split, while the token-space region split has little effect. The study does not report that these choices induce grokking.
record.code_released: not stated; the text says the code URL would be disclosed upon acceptance.
record.problems: The main results use a random split with 12288 training examples out of 16384; the study does not sweep smaller training sets. Results are averaged over five runs, but no error bars or other uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No sweep of training-set size. No small training fractions, where V1 predicts the delay. No dependence of delay on data size.
No progress measures or circuit-formation dynamics over training.
No non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation.
No weight-decay manipulation, critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
No comparison of learned algorithms across runs. The two architectures are compared only by accuracy.
No optimizer or numerical-precision controls bearing on the delay.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label is downgraded to limits_scope. V1 ties the delay to small training sets. The original Power et al. results also show near-immediate generalization at high training fractions, so the absence of grokking at 75% of all 16384 examples is consistent with V1's size dependence rather than a contradiction. The random-output control (validation flat over 1000 epochs) is rightly excluded: the task has no generalizable structure. The Appendix C plain-order curves show slower, less stable learning but no reported train/validation gap, so they are not added.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not sweep training-set size or test whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks.

rows.subject: original encoder-decoder Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Train on binary addition and track training and validation sequence accuracy over epochs.

conditions.value: random; 12288 training examples and 4096 validation examples

rows.measure: Training and validation sequence accuracy over epochs
rows.value: Addition learned in less than 50 epochs; validation accuracy was very close to training accuracy, and the curves were almost overlapped. The authors state that no grokking was observed.
rows.uncertainty: Results averaged over five runs; no error bars or other uncertainty stated.
rows.note: The reported accuracy pattern lacks the long gap between saturated training accuracy and a later test-accuracy rise described by V1.
rows.check: Row is accurate. The 75% training fraction (12288/16384), no explicit weight decay (Adam, dropout 0.1) and a ~50-epoch run belong in the conditions. These are settings where V1 itself predicts little or no delay.

relationships.condition: Binary addition and multiplication, 75% random training split, encoder-decoder Transformer (Adam) and nanoGPT (AdamW)
relationships.reason: Training and validation curves overlap with no delayed test rise (r1–r4). This shows the jump is not universal on algorithmic tasks, but it occurs at a large training fraction where V1 predicts little delay, so it does not challenge V1.
relationships.display_finding: Training and validation curves overlapped for both architectures and operations, without a delayed test-accuracy rise.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
